title: A Maine couple grew their own wedding flowers in a 30-by-50-foot backyard garden after estimating florist costs could reach $5,000
summary: Mariah Reading and David Mainero decided to grow their own wedding flowers after learning that a single bridal bouquet would cost $400.
body:
PC: Instagram (mariahreading)

Mariah Reading and David Mainero decided to grow their own wedding flowers after learning that a single bridal bouquet would cost $400. The couple planted a 30-by-50-foot garden in Reading’s parents’ backyard in Hampden, Maine, in May 2026, hoping to avoid spending thousands of dollars on flowers for their September wedding. According to The PEOPLE, the garden had five long rows of blooms, including dahlias and amaranth, which they planned to use for bouquets, boutonnieres, and other arrangements. The project cost about $1,000 and required months of care, research, and patience. By their wedding on September 26, the flowers had become an important part of the celebration, giving the couple a personal way to prepare for their marriage.

How a couple saved thousands by growing their own wedding flowers

Reading began exploring options for a wildflower-style bridal bouquet and was quoted $400 for the bouquet alone. As the couple was also saving to buy a house in the area, she estimated that wedding flowers could cost between $3,000 and $5,000, leading them to grow their own instead. Reading and Mainero created a garden in her parents’ backyard. The project cost about $1,000, including a rented rototiller, loam soil, seafood compost, locally ordered seeds and chicken wire to keep deer and other animals away.

Reading began planting in mid-May, several months before their September 26 wedding. The couple wanted flowers that suited their colourful, relaxed celebration without spending thousands on professionally arranged blooms.

How the couple chose their wedding flowers and learned to grow them

Reading wanted the flowers to reflect the transition between summer and autumn. Her chosen colours included vermilion, bright red, orange, lilac, soft purple, green and chartreuse. Amaranth provided long, dangling shapes, while dahlias added deep maroon, plum and magenta tones. The wedding theme was vibrant, whimsical and fun, and the garden was planned around that vision. However, Reading had never grown a full-scale flower garden before. Although her parents had grown plants when she was growing up, cultivating flowers on this scale was completely new to her. She sought advice from a gardening friend, researched how to grow the plants, and learned to accept that not everything would go according to plan. Some flowers failed to grow as expected, while the white gladiolas bloomed and finished before the wedding.

How homegrown flowers and creative exchanges shaped their wedding

Reading and Mainero spent the summer tending the flowers, learning about gardening and adjusting to the changing seasons and weather. Reading said, “I just think growing your own flowers is so rewarding on multiple levels, and I think a lot of people kind of were picking up on the metaphor of tending to your relationship and adding water and providing for it and giving it sunlight.”The garden also allowed the couple to make other parts of their wedding personal. Reading’s college friend hand-sewed her wedding dress, and Reading made a landscape painting in return. Her sister-in-law prepared a buttercream amaretto cake with strawberry rhubarb filling and decorated it with flowers from the garden, according to The PEOPLE.Reading also exchanged painting lessons for two full days of photography. Friends and family helped with other details, while the couple reused and sourced items rather than buying everything new. Their wedding arch was built from wooden boat components found through Facebook Marketplace.

Why growing their own flowers made the wedding more personal

On the morning of their wedding, Reading went into the garden to pick her own bouquet, while Mainero selected his boutonniere. Reading described the moment as especially meaningful and one she expected to remember forever. The couple’s approximately 40 guests also experienced the garden, with some picking flowers during the celebration. After the ceremony, Reading and Mainero took a canoe ride, returning to an activity connected to their first date. They had met while working as park rangers at Isle Royale National Park in Michigan, and their first date had been a canoe trip. Reading said the garden helped the couple build a closer connection with the flowers used in their wedding. She also acknowledged that having the time and flexibility to care for the plants was a privilege, as she worked as a freelance artist that summer.

title: A Scottish Labrador once trained for mountain rescue learned to sniff out an invasive marine creature called ‘sea vomit’; after finding hundreds of colonies, Sgiath was named Animal of the Year
summary: A black Labrador from the Scottish Highlands has found an unusual new calling beneath the waves, and it has earned her international recognition.
body:
A black Labrador from the Scottish Highlands has found an unusual new calling beneath the waves, and it has earned her international recognition. Sgiath, a six-year-old dog once trained for mountain rescue, has become the first dog in the world trained to detect an invasive marine organism nicknamed “sea vomit”. Her remarkable ability to locate the creature, even when it is concealed among other marine life, has helped her win the Animal of the Year award from the International Fund for Animal Welfare (IFAW).The award recognises more than an extraordinary canine skill. It highlights a creative approach to marine conservation, where a dog’s powerful sense of smell could help scientists identify a damaging invasive species before it spreads further. Sgiath’s work offers conservationists another way to monitor vulnerable coastal environments and protect native marine life.

From mountain rescue missions to an unexpected underwater mission

Sgiath’s career took a surprising turn when her handler, marine ecologist Dr Texa Sim, began exploring whether a dog could help address a problem facing Scotland’s west coast. Sim, originally from Glasgow and now based near Glencoe, was working on a native oyster restoration project when she became increasingly concerned about invasive marine species.

One species in particular caught her attention: Didemnum vexillum, commonly called carpet sea squirt and sometimes referred to as “sea vomit”. The organism can spread across harbours, oyster farms and other marine structures, forming dense colonies that smother native species and disrupt local ecosystems. Detecting it is not always straightforward. Identification can require specialist laboratory work and DNA testing, making early detection challenging for people managing marine sites. Sim wondered whether a dog’s exceptional sense of smell could offer a faster and more practical way to locate the organism. The idea was experimental. Dogs are widely known for detecting scents in search-and-rescue operations, but using one to identify a marine organism presented a different challenge. Sim began training Sgiath to recognise the target species among a range of similar smells. The early results surprised her. “The first time I asked her to identify the target species among lots of similar scents, she went straight to it,” Sim recalled. “That was the moment I thought: maybe this is actually going to work.” Sgiath’s performance helped turn an uncertain experiment into a promising conservation project. According to Sim, the work has resulted in the detection of hundreds of colonies, demonstrating how scent detection could complement existing monitoring methods.

How one dog could help protect marine ecosystems

Carpet sea squirt is a concern because it can establish itself quickly and spread over surfaces in coastal waters. Once dense colonies take hold, they can smother other organisms and create difficulties for marine habitats and industries such as oyster farming. Finding an invasive species early gives conservationists a better opportunity to assess the problem and decide how to respond. Sgiath’s ability to identify its scent could help direct attention to areas that need closer examination, potentially reducing the time and effort required to locate colonies. Sim has been candid about the experimental nature of the work. title: An 84-year-old Australian pensioner left his home to an online wife he never met; a court ruled she did not exist and awarded his estate to his daughter
summary: Clifford Stanley Perrin died in Maryborough Hospital on Christmas Eve 2025, aged 84 and divorced.
body:
Image AI generated

Clifford Stanley Perrin died in Maryborough Hospital on Christmas Eve 2025, aged 84 and divorced. He had been the victim of a scam that depleted his finances, leaving his estate with one asset: a small property in Hervey Bay, which was subject to a reverse mortgage. According to the Supreme Court of Queensland judgment in the Will of Clifford Stanley Perrin [2026] QSC 247, his handmade will named the scammer, whose purported name was Stella Helena Perrin, as executor and beneficiary. On 24 September 2026, Treston J found that she did not exist and that her appointment and the gift to her failed.

How did a fake online lover target an Australian pensioner’s home

Mr Perrin was born on 24 February 1941 and did not finish high school, but worked in a variety of occupations during his working life. His father died in about 1986 and his mother in 2004, and in the years before her death he was her full-time carer. In 2005 he retired to a modest home in Point Vernon, Hervey Bay, where he lived until he went into hospital before his death. He was briefly married between April 1971 and June 1976, and the marriage ended in divorce. The judgment records that his only daughter was born shortly after the marriage in 1971. While she was growing up she was told her father was deceased, and she learned otherwise in her twenties.

Around 2010, a DNA test showed a 99.99 per cent chance that Mr Perrin was her father. The court noted that the relationship was "not a particularly close one" and that, after about 2019, he appears to have stopped contacting her entirely. In about 2012, he befriended a local bus driver, Mr Kim, who began picking him up two or three times a week. Mr Kim observed that Mr Perrin was a lonely man who lived alone and did not appear to have a regular circle of friends.

How did a fake online wife convince a pensioner he was married to her

Unknown to both his daughter and Mr Kim, Mr Perrin had one other friend, a woman called Stella Helena Bennett. Records obtained after his death indicate that he met her over the internet in about 2012. She told him she was born in 1976, a former fashion model from an upper middle-class family in New York, who lived in the town of Massena. At that time, Mr Perrin was a 71-year-old pensioner with significantly impaired vision who could no longer drive. According to the court, he had never travelled to New York and had never met Stella. Even so, on 25 April 2013 he considered that he had married her. In an email to a friend on 6 May 2013, headed "Take a seat before you read this, Pete", he described Stella as his wife and said she was coming to live in Point Vernon. Stella told him they had been married by proxy and later sent him a copy of a marriage certificate, which the court found to be a forgery. Around the time they connected online, she also said she had received a large inheritance from her father, held in New York by a Zimbabwe-based company, which she could not access until tax was paid. The judgment records that she sought his financial assistance and identity information to pay the Internal Revenue Service, and promised to move to Hervey Bay with the balance of the funds. In 2014, she told him she had moved to Kuala Lumpur and become a Malaysian citizen. She later said Malaysian taxes were blocking the inheritance and gave him an "inheritance tax bond disclosure" and a letter purportedly from "MPI Generali Insurans Bhd". The court found both documents were false, and stressed that there was no suggestion the legitimate company had any part in producing them.

How did a pensioner’s fake online wife obtain his money and inheritance

Stella extracted various funds from Mr Perrin over time. The evidence shows she asked him to transfer money to accounts in other people's names, send Bitcoin, send iTunes Gift Cards and Steam Wallet Cards, provide cash to unspecified third parties, and mail new SIM cards or iPhones to her. At different times she also obtained his credit card information, bank details, myGov account details and identity documents. In May 2024 his own bank blocked a transfer, and a bank employee told him the receiving account was associated with a scam. The court found that Mr Perrin suggested Stella simply prove her identity, but that she instead suggested he tell the bank he was sending money to a family member who needed medical help. The will is dated 3 May 2024, although the evidence suggests it may have been executed on 4 May 2024. It was witnessed in the presence of two justices of the peace. The court described it as a handmade document in two parts. Part A revokes earlier wills and appoints Stella, "my wife", as executor and trustee, recording that she lived in Kuala Lumpur. It also bequeaths the bulk of the estate to her. A further dot point provides that if Stella should "pass away before my death", the entire estate goes to his daughter. The court found that Mr Perrin was not shown to lack testamentary capacity and that the will was duly executed. It found no earlier will.

How did a court expose an Australian pensioner’s fake online wife

The court gave nine reasons for finding that Stella was "either not a real person or does not exist at all". They included the improbable nature of the supposed match, and the marriage certificate, which bore no seal, named "Fresno County of New York" although Fresno County is in California, referred to "New York State Republic", and misspelt the bride's name. The applicant's solicitors also confirmed with the Massena Town Hall that no such marriage certificate was registered. The judge accepted evidence that, after Mr Perrin's death, Stella refused to prove her identity when asked, asked for money first, and then deleted the message exchange. The court also found that during his lifetime she suggested he gift money immediately rather than wait to die, and that she repeatedly pressed him to take out a reverse mortgage on his property. Applying the Briginshaw standard, the judge concluded that the evidence strongly supported the inference that Stella had perpetrated a romance scam.On the legal question, Treston J applied the rule in Jones v Westcomb, concluding that Mr Perrin must have intended the gift over to his daughter to operate if Stella never existed. The judge relied on the wording of the clause, which was functionally the same as in Re the Will of William Ian Southey [2025] VSC 801, and on emails in which Mr Perrin recorded suspicions of Stella in January 2015 and again in August 2024. The judge said that, had the rule not applied, the parts of the will affected by his false assumption about her character or identity would have been severed, following Kennell v Abbott. The court ordered that the will be pronounced in solemn form of law and declared that the applicant, Tanya Maree Stankovich, was entitled to probate as executor and to the residue as sole beneficiary. It also ordered that costs be paid out of the estate on the indemnity basis.

title: A 10-year-old New Jersey girl wrote a poem inspired by her Colombian heritage; her work was picked from thousands of entries to finish in the national contest’s Top 10
summary: Luisa's poem uses the colours of the Colombian flag to reflect her Colombian American identity.
body:
Luisa's poem uses the colours of the Colombian flag to reflect her Colombian American identity.

A 10-year-old girl from New Jersey has been named among the Top 10 winners of a national poetry competition in the United States for a poem inspired by her Colombian heritage. Luisa Gonzalez, a fifth-grade student from Cherry Hill, received the recognition for her poem All Stitched Together, which was selected from thousands of entries submitted by students across the country. Luisa secured a place in the grades 4 to 6 category of Creative Communication's Summer 2026 poetry contest. Her poem, listed on the competition's official website, draws on the colours of the Colombian flag to explore her identity as a Colombian American. Through the idea of different colours being joined together, she describes how her two cultural backgrounds form part of who she is. According to South Jersey Media, the idea came to Luisa when she was thinking about the Colombian flag and the way its colours fit together. She wanted her poem to reflect her cultural background while encouraging others to take pride in their own identities. Luisa had participated in the competition several times before and received honourable mentions, but had never reached the Top 10.

How Luisa found out about her poetry award

Reaching the Top 10 was a goal Luisa had been working towards for some time. Her mother, Lauren Gonzalez, knew how much it meant to her because she had continued submitting poems despite not securing a place among the top winners in previous attempts.

Lauren shared the competition results with Luisa one morning while she was preparing for school. The news left her excited, particularly because she had finally achieved something she had been trying to accomplish."A smile spread across my face and I jumped up and down!" Luisa told South Jersey Media. "I was so glad I won top 10 because I have never won top 10 before in that contest, so I was thrilled."

How a love for books led Luisa to poetry

Luisa's interest in poetry developed from her earlier attempts at storytelling and songwriting. She was already making her own books in first grade, using folded sheets of printer paper for a series she called The Brave Girl Series. In the following years, she began writing songs, and it was a suggestion from her aunt that encouraged her to explore poetry. Reading has also been an important part of her routine. Her mother told South Jersey Media that Luisa frequently reads during everyday activities, including car journeys to soccer practice. Her interest in books and writing eventually led her parents to encourage her participation in poetry competitions and public readings.

Luisa Gonzalez's winning poem (Screengrab: Creative communications' official website)

"I first started writing songs before I wrote poems!" Luisa explained. "Once my aunt remarked I would be a great poet after reading my songs, I decided to write poetry as well as songs."With encouragement from her family, Luisa began taking part in local writing competitions and sharing her work at open mic events at Inkwood Books in Haddonfield. Her literary interests extend beyond poetry. She admires the works of Langston Hughes and Maya Angelou, as well as songwriter Dolly Parton and Harry Potter author J K Rowling.

What is Luisa's winning poem All Stitched Together about?

Luisa's family continues to maintain a connection with Colombia, where her grandparents live. They travel there every other year and remain in contact through virtual conversations between visits. Her grandparents also visit the family in the United States. Spanish is part of family life, with her father, Francisco, speaking the language to the children at home. Luisa and one of her younger brothers also take Spanish classes locally. These family experiences form part of the cultural background Luisa wanted to express in All Stitched Together. Through the colours of the Colombian flag, she explored what it means to grow up with both Colombian and American identities."Hispanic Heritage means so much to me," she said. "It means to be proud of yourself as a Hispanic, and to be you."

From local poetry competitions to national recognition

Luisa had experience presenting her work to audiences even before receiving the national award. She has taken part in community events, including the Collingswood Hispanic Heritage Festival, and also secured first place in Collingswood's Youth Poetry Contest. However, speaking in front of an audience was initially difficult for her. She said that she worried about making mistakes, especially when presenting one of her poems in Spanish. With experience, she became more comfortable reading her work publicly. Her growing confidence has also been visible at school. According to her mother, Luisa had previously preferred not to tell her school about a local poetry award. This year, she decided to share her achievement with her principal, who responded with encouraging emails and video messages. Luisa, who has three younger brothers, hopes to continue writing as she grows older. She wants to become a teacher, poet and author, and hopes to encourage other children to develop their interests. "I would love to encourage others to stay curious," she said. According to Creative Communication's official website, the other nine students selected as Top 10 winners in the grades 4 to 6 category of the Summer 2026 poetry contest were Patti-Rose Gonzalez, Eugene Wong, Eli Johnson, Hanifa Khan, Henry Wang, Aila Adeline, Anna Zhao, Jayceon Jones and Luke Feirstein.

title: Compact, clever, cinematic: How the Mini stole big scenes in movies
summary: No car has squeezed more personality into so little metal than the Mini Cooper.
body:
Long before high-octane spectacle became the norm, the little car Mini Cooper proved that wit could outpace brute force.

No car has squeezed more personality into so little metal than the Mini Cooper. It became a style icon almost as soon as it launched in 1959, arriving in a world obsessed with tailfins and excess and promptly rewriting the script. Here was a car that did not shout for attention, yet stole every glance. It slipped into tight corners, darted through narrow streets, and made agility feel like attitude. Cinema caught on early. The Mini first appeared on the big screen in A Shot in the Dark (1964), but the swagger of the sixties sealed its image. Pop royalty such as The Beatles made it a statement off screen, while even Enzo Ferrari was charmed enough to own one. This was not just a car. It was a mood. Then came the chase. Few films have used a car as playfully, or as precisely, as The Italian Job (1969), where the Mini turned tight alleys and staircases into a playground. Long before high-octane spectacle became the norm, this little car proved that wit could outpace brute force. Decades later, whether weaving through traffic or punctuating a scene with its cheeky presence, the Mini remains cinema’s favourite underdog on four wheels.

body:
PC: JAKKS Pacific press release

Horror icons Ghost Face, Jason Voorhees, Pinhead and Billy the Puppet are getting fashion-doll makeovers as toy maker JAKKS Pacific prepares to launch its new Doll Haus of Dread collection. The range features 11-inch collectable dolls inspired by characters from Scream, Friday the 13th, Hellraiser and Saw, complete with distinctive outfits, signature accessories and nine points of articulation. Two versions of Ghost Face will be available, including a limited-edition doll with an embellished mask sold exclusively online. According to a JAKKS Pacific press release, each doll will retail for $39.97 and launch exclusively at Walmart and Walmart.com in autumn 2026.

How is Ghost Face getting a fashion-doll makeover

The collection includes two versions of Ghost Face, the masked killer from the Scream franchise. One doll features the character's familiar hooded silhouette, while a limited-edition version will be available exclusively through Walmart. The special edition features a mask decorated with embellishments, offering a different look from the classic design. The release describes the dolls as combining franchise-inspired clothing with carefully designed accessories.

Both versions draw on Ghost Face's established appearance in the horror films, while the limited-edition figure introduces a more elaborate mask. The collection is intended for horror enthusiasts and collectors interested in entertainment-inspired fashion dolls.

How is Jason Voorhees getting a fashion-doll makeover

Jason Voorhees, the central figure associated with the Friday the 13th horror franchise and the Jason Universe brand, is also part of the debut collection. His doll takes inspiration from the slasher and summer camp themes associated with the character and comes with his signature hockey mask. The range reinterprets well-known horror characters through fashion and collectable design. The Jason figure follows the collection's 11-inch format and includes nine points of articulation. Its outfit and accessories draw on the character's established horror identity while presenting him as a fashion doll.

How are Pinhead and Billy the Puppet getting fashion makeovers

Pinhead, the character from the Hellraiser franchise, is presented in a Cenobite-inspired gown. The design brings the character's horror background into the fashion-doll format, with the outfit forming a central part of the figure's appearance. The doll is included alongside Ghost Face, Jason Voorhees and Billy the Puppet in the initial release. Billy the Puppet from Saw is dressed in a pinstripe tuxedo suit, reflecting the character's recognisable formal appearance. The figure is part of the same 11-inch collection and features the articulated construction used across the range. The announcement highlights franchise-inspired fashions and signature accessories as key elements of the dolls.

What is the Doll Haus of Dread collection

Doll Haus of Dread is the first release in a broader Doll Haus initiative that JAKKS Pacific intends to develop into a collector-focused destination. According to the company, future collections will span fandom-related properties, entertainment exclusives and collaborations. The plans extend beyond individual products to include a wider range of offerings for collectors. The company also said it intends to develop the collector experience through direct-to-consumer exclusives, behind-the-scenes content and a growing presence at conventions and events. The initial horror collection will be available at Walmart stores and the Walmart website in autumn 2026.

How is JAKKS Pacific reimagining horror icons as fashion dolls

Dominick Lisi, senior vice-president of marketing at JAKKS Pacific, said the collection was created to reinterpret established horror characters while retaining connections to their original franchises.“With Doll Haus of Dread™, we're reimagining some of horror's most legendary figures as collectable works of art, blending authentic franchise storytelling with elevated fashion, sculptural detail, and artistic interpretation,” Lisi said in the announcement.He added that the dolls were intended to reflect the characters, films and cultural impact of the horror genre. The collection brings together licensed entertainment properties and fashion-doll styling, with the initial range focusing on four well-known horror figures and two versions of Ghost Face.JAKKS Pacific, headquartered in Santa Monica, California, designs, manufactures and markets toys and consumer products internationally. Its portfolio includes proprietary brands and products based on licensed entertainment properties. With Doll Haus of Dread, the company is introducing a new collector line built around horror characters, with further sub-collections planned as part of the broader Doll Haus concept.

title: Dead fish in ‘cleanest’ Yamuna stretch in city raise alarm over pollution after monsoon
keywords: South Asia Network on Dams Rivers and People
summary: Dead fish found in Delhi’s “cleanest” Yamuna stretch near Burari after monsoon spark pollution fears; groups urge DPCC probe, sampling, and real-time monitoring.
body:
Countless dead fish littering the banks of the Yamuna River near Wazirabad, prompting urgent discussions about pollution

NEW DELHI: Visuals of hundreds of dead fish and many more gasping for oxygen in Yamuna upstream of Wazirabad have raised fresh concerns over the river’s pollution levels. The alarming development comes soon after the monsoon, when the river is expected to have adequate water along with cleaner inflows from upstream.TOI had recently reported a spike in pollution levels in the river in Sept, raising questions about why water quality remains so poor even after the monsoon. Over the past few days, fishermen had been reporting a rising stink from the river before large numbers of dead fish were found floating Tuesday in its main channel near Burari – between Palla and Wazirabad – which is often considered its cleanest stretch in Delhi. Such events have occurred in the past, often during summer when the reduced river flow limits the dilution of pollutants. Post-monsoon, the river, however, has water, raising questions about what could have triggered the deaths.In a letter to Delhi Pollution Control Committee (DPCC), environmental group Earth Warrior sought an immediate investigation and water sampling at upstream locations. It called for testing dissolved oxygen, biochemical and chemical oxygen demand, faecal coliform, heavy metals and toxic substances, and identifying drains or industrial units discharging untreated effluents.

The group also sought public disclosure of the findings and real-time monitoring of major drains.“Similar fish deaths were reported near Burari in May 2025 and July 2024,” stated the letter while warning that Burari lies upstream of Wazirabad barrage, and the incident could have implications for Delhi’s drinking water source. Bhim Singh Rawat of South Asia Network on Dams, Rivers and People said the recurring deaths in a “relatively cleaner stretch” were deeply concerning. “If this is from pollution, then adverse effect may impact Delhi’s potable water as well,” he said, calling for an investigation to find the exact cause. Rawat flagged restricted environmental flows and untreated discharges from drains, including Drain no. 2 in Panipat and Dhanaura drain in Haryana, as possible contributors. He said industrial pollution could also be a factor.

The incident follows DPCC’s Sept water-quality analysis, which recorded high pollution levels at several locations, including an elevated biochemical oxygen demand and faecal coliform count at ISBT Bridge. No response was available from DPCC on the recent incident.

title: ‘Muslim youths at venue’: Right-wing groups disrupt garba event, Congress leader shoved on stage
summary: A garba event organised at the Civil Lines hockey ground in Durg turned tense on Wednesday night after Bajrang Dal and VHP workers objected to the alleged presence of Muslim youths at the venue, leading to a scuffle on stage in which Congress city district president and former mayor Dheeraj Bakliwal was shoved. Videos
body:
RAIPUR: A garba event organised at the Civil Lines hockey ground in Durg turned tense on Wednesday night after Bajrang Dal and VHP workers objected to the alleged presence of Muslim youths at the venue, leading to a scuffle on stage in which Congress city district president and former mayor Dheeraj Bakliwal was shoved. Videos of the incident, showing arguments, pushing and a brief melee, later circulated on social media. The dispute had reportedly begun after an NSUI office-bearer, Adil Khan, shared a promotional poster for the event on social media, mentioning free entry passes.On Wednesday night, members of right wing outfits reached the venue and went up to the stage. One of the organisers’ opponents addressed the gathering and objected to the entry of Muslims into the garba venue. They were asked not to disrupt the programme. The exchange escalated and several people began pushing each other. In one of the videos, a man is seen shoving Bakliwal before others at the venue intervene. Bakliwal later said the event was free and open to anyone who came with faith and respect for the festival, and accused some people of deliberately disrupting it.VHP functionary Ramlochan Tiwari, however, said the organisation opposed the participation of Muslim youths in garba and demanded tighter entry checks.

Police have registered a case on the complaint of the organising committee and are examining CCTV footage to identify those involved. title: 'Entire movement orchestrated at Elon Musk's behest': Brij Bhushan Singh on CJP's Tiranga march
summary: BJP leader Brij Bhushan Sharan Singh on Friday alleged that Elon Musk was orchestrating the Cockroach Janata Party’s (CJP) “Lehra Do Tiranga”
body:
File photo: Brij Bhushan Singh and Elon Musk

NEW DELHI: BJP leader Brij Bhushan Sharan Singh on Friday alleged that Elon Musk was orchestrating the Cockroach Janata Party’s (CJP) “Lehra Do Tiranga” protest, calling it a conspiracy against India as the party prepared to hold demonstrations in Delhi and Mumbai.“This entire movement is being orchestrated at his (Elon Musk) behest. It is a massive conspiracy against our nation,” Singh said in Unnao, Uttar Pradesh. He alleged that India was being compared with Bangladesh and Pakistan and claimed the march was intended to intimidate the Supreme Court. Singh did not provide evidence for the allegations. The CJP has called for a flag march at Central Park in Delhi’s Connaught Place at 5pm on Friday, October 16, while its Mumbai unit has received police permission to hold a demonstration at Azad Maidan from 10am to 5pm.

CJP protests arrests of leaders

The proposed demonstrations follow the arrests of CJP co-conveners Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das after they reached Jantar Mantar in Delhi. The two were subsequently remanded to five days of judicial custody by a special executive magistrate.CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke has urged citizens to join the Delhi march, maintaining that waving the national flag is a democratic right. The party has also called for parallel Tiranga marches in other cities.

In Mumbai, CJP in-charge Pranay Ahire said the demonstration was intended to assert the party’s patriotism.“We want to show the government that we are the real patriots, not the fake patriots or fake deshbhakts that this government is,” Ahire said in an Instagram video.

Ahire said the party had permission for only a one-day protest and ruled out confirming any indefinite sit-in.

Security tightened in Delhi

Police sources said several companies of paramilitary forces would be deployed in and around Connaught Place and Jantar Mantar ahead of the proposed Delhi gathering. Barricades are expected at strategic locations, with police regulating the movement of protesters and commuters.A senior police officer said Connaught Place is not a designated protest site. Jantar Mantar has also been denotified as a designated protest site, the officer said, adding that demonstrations can be held at Ramlila Maidan, Burari Ground or CBD Ground after obtaining the required permission.
